rejected.title: The crisis of 1787 and 1788
card: By 1787 the crown was short of money. Finance minister Calonne proposed a tax on land that nobles and clergy would also have to pay.

Calonne first called an Assembly of Notables, a hand-picked group of nobles and clergy, to approve the plan. They refused. The Parlements, the high law courts staffed by nobles, later also refused to register new taxes.

This was a revolt by the privileged orders, who wanted to protect their own tax exemptions. Many of them said only the Estates-General, a national assembly of the three estates, could approve new taxes.

On 7 June 1788, in the Day of Tiles at Grenoble, townspeople threw roof tiles at royal troops to back their Parlement. In August 1788 the king agreed to call the Estates-General, which had not met since 1614, for May 1789.
rejected.remember: Nobles blocked tax reform and crowds backed them, so the king had to call the Estates-General.

a.q: Why did the Assembly of Notables and the Parlements resist the crown's tax plans in 1787 and 1788?
opts: They wanted to keep their own exemptions from tax
They wanted the Third Estate to gain equal votes
They believed the crown had no need for more money
They wanted the king replaced by a republic
a.why: The plan would have made nobles and clergy pay a land tax, so they defended their privileges. They did not deny the crown's money problems, and they were not seeking to help the Third Estate or end the monarchy.
a.clue: Who would have paid the new land tax?

b.q: In 1788 a crowd in Grenoble threw roof tiles at royal troops. What does this Day of Tiles show about the crisis?
opts: Opposition to the crown had spread beyond the nobles
The nobles had accepted the crown's tax reform
Peasants had begun attacking noble estates
The king had already called the Estates-General
b.why: Townspeople backed their Parlement against the crown's troops, so resistance was no longer limited to nobles. The crowd was supporting a noble court, not attacking nobles, and the nobles were still refusing the tax plan. The king agreed to call the Estates-General in August, after the Day of Tiles, not before.
b.clue: Think about who threw the tiles and whom they supported.

problems.detail: The usual date for the king's commitment to the Estates-General is 8 August 1788, when the meeting was fixed for May 1789. A decree of 5 July 1788 only asked for advice on how to hold it. 'In July 1788 the king agreed' can be defended but may clash with textbook dates, so 'In August 1788' (or 'In mid-1788') is safer.
